content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Wrongful confinement (old 340/342): restraint that prevents a person from proceeding beyond circumscribing limits. Confinement is a species of restraint. BNS restatement of IPC 340 / 342–348. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 127 is the rule on “Wrongful confinement”. The section provides that (1) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said “wrongfully to confine” that person. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 127 exists so that “Wrongful confinement” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
127. (1) Whoever wrongfully restrains any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceedings beyond certain circumscribing limits, is said “wrongfully to confine” that person

(2) Whoever wrongfully confines any person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both

(3) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for three days, or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both

(4) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for ten days or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees

(5) Whoever keeps any person in wrongful confinement, knowing that a writ for the liberation of that person has been duly issued, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years in addition to any term of imprisonment to which he may be liable under any other section of this Chapter and shall also be liable to fine

(6) Whoever wrongfully confines any person in such manner as to indicate an intention that the confinement of such person may not be known to any person interested in the person so confined, or to any public servant, or that the place of such confinement may not be known to or discovered by any such person or public servant as hereinbefore mentioned, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years in addition to any other punishment to which he may be liable for such wrongful confinement and shall also be liable to fine

(7) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined, or from any person interested in the person confined, any property or valuable security or of constraining the person confined or any person interested in such person to do anything illegal or to give any information which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine

(8) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined or any person interested in the person confined any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the person confined or any person interested in the person confined to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine

Of criminal force and assault

2. (2) Whoever wrongfully confines any person shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both
3. (3) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for three days, or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both
4. (4) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for ten days or more, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to five years, and shall also be liable to fine which shall not be less than ten thousand rupees
5. (5) Whoever keeps any person in wrongful confinement, knowing that a writ for the liberation of that person has been duly issued, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to two years in addition to any term of imprisonment to which he may be liable under any other section of this Chapter and shall also be liable to fine
6. (6) Whoever wrongfully confines any person in such manner as to indicate an intention that the confinement of such person may not be known to any person interested in the person so confined, or to any public servant, or that the place of such confinement may not be known to or discovered by any such person or public servant as hereinbefore mentioned, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years in addition to any other punishment to which he may be liable for such wrongful confinement and shall also be liable to fine
7. (7) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined, or from any person interested in the person confined, any property or valuable security or of constraining the person confined or any person interested in such person to do anything illegal or to give any information which may facilitate the commission of an offence, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine
8. (8) Whoever wrongfully confines any person for the purpose of extorting from the person confined or any person interested in the person confined any confession or any information which may lead to the detection of an offence or misconduct, or for the purpose of constraining the person confined or any person interested in the person confined to restore or to cause the restoration of any property or valuable security or to satisfy any claim or demand, or to give information which may lead to the restoration of any property or valuable security, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to three years, and shall also be liable to fine
9. Of criminal force and assault

Statutory illustrations
Illustration (a). A causes Z to go within a walled space, and locks Z in. Z is thus prevented from proceeding in any direction beyond the circumscribing line of wall. A wrongfully confines Z

Exam use: quote illustration (a), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 127 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

Illustration (b). A places men with firearms at the outlets of a building, and tells Z that they will fire at Z if Z attempts to leave the building. A wrongfully confines Z

Exam use: quote illustration (b), then write which ingredient of BNS s. 127 it proves. Copying the illustration without that mapping sentence does not score.

learningObjectives: Master the definition of wrongful confinement under BNS s. 127 as total circumscribed restraint.
Analyze the graduated punishment framework: base confinement (up to 1 year/₹5,000), 3+ days (up to 2 years), and 10+ days (up to 3 years and fine).
Examine aggravated forms: confinement after writ issued, in secret, or for extortion of property/confession.
Contrast wrongful confinement with wrongful restraint.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 127 defines wrongful confinement as wrongfully restraining any person in such a manner as to prevent that person from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing limits, punishable under sub-section (2) with imprisonment up to one year, fine up to ₹5,000, or both, with escalating penalties for confinement exceeding three days (sub-section 3), exceeding ten days (sub-section 4), confinement in secret (sub-section 6), and confinement for extortion or forced confessions (sub-sections 7-8).
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Protects total bodily liberty by penalizing the creation of an inescapable circumscribing perimeter (physical or psychological) that completely deprives a person of freedom of movement.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 127 (consolidating IPC ss. 340, 342, 343, 344, 345, 346, 347, 348).
Sub-section (1): Definitive formula — wrongful restraint preventing proceeding beyond circumscribing limits.
Sub-section (2): Base punishment — imprisonment up to one year, or fine up to ₹5,000, or both.
Sub-section (3): Confinement for three or more days — imprisonment up to two years, or fine, or both.
Sub-section (4): Confinement for ten or more days — imprisonment up to three years, and fine.
Sub-section (5): Confinement of person for whose liberation writ has been issued — imprisonment up to two years in addition to other terms.
Sub-section (6): Confinement in secret — imprisonment up to two years in addition.
Sub-sections (7)-(8): Confinement for extortion of property/confession — imprisonment up to three years, and fine.
Statutory illustration: A causes Z to go within a walled space and locks Z in; Z is wrongfully confined.
essentialIngredients: The restraint was total, preventing the victim from proceeding beyond certain circumscribing boundaries.
The accused acted voluntarily without lawful justification.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 127 unifies the entire cluster of wrongful confinement offences from the old IPC (Sections 340 to 348) into an eight-tier integrated framework. The distinguishing feature of confinement is that the restraint is total: the victim cannot move in ANY direction outside the defined perimeter. The perimeter does not have to be physical walls; it can be an open field encircled by armed guards, a moving vehicle where doors are locked, or a room where an unarmed victim is held under fear of immediate shooting. Sub-sections (3) and (4) establish progressive sentences based on duration (3+ days: 2 years; 10+ days: 3 years). Sub-sections (5) to (8) impose aggravated liability when confinement defies court writs (habeas corpus), is conducted in clandestine secrecy, or is used to extort property or force confessions.
examples: Teaching example (Locked in room): An employer locks a domestic worker inside a storeroom overnight to prevent her from quitting. The worker has no means of egress. This is wrongful confinement under s. 127(2).

Teaching example (Confinement for ten days): An accused keeps a kidnapped business partner inside an abandoned farmhouse for twelve continuous days. Under s. 127(4), the punishment extends up to three years imprisonment and fine.
distinctions: Wrongful Confinement (s. 127) vs Wrongful Restraint (s. 126): Restraint blocks one direction; Confinement blocks all directions (circumscribing boundaries).
Wrongful Confinement vs Kidnapping (s. 137): Kidnapping requires taking out of India or lawful guardianship; Confinement merely requires total physical detention of any person anywhere.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who forced an employee into an office, locked the only exit door, and took the keys for four hours to compel the employee to sign an audit report is guilty under s. 127.
Rule: Preventing a person from proceeding beyond circumscribing limits without lawful authority constitutes wrongful confinement under BNS s. 127.
Application: The employee was totally enclosed in the office with no exit available.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of wrongful confinement under BNS s. 127(2) and (8).
